newsitem.title: BELGIUM: WORKERS, BELGIUM ATTACK RENAULT OVER PLANT CLOSURE.
newsitem.headline: WORKERS, BELGIUM ATTACK RENAULT OVER PLANT CLOSURE.

text.p: French car maker Renault SA came under fire on Monday for deciding to close its plant near Brussels as thousands of workers took to the streets and Belgian authorities said they would sue the company for procedural breaches.

In Paris, unions called for a one-hour strike at all Renault plants in France, Belgium and Spain to protest against the closure of the Vilvoorde factory near Brussels, and at reports that many jobs would also go in France.
The workforce of Renault Industrie Belgique, which totals 3,100, marched through Brussels with about 1,000 workers from other threatened factories.
Workers chanted "Renault stays open" and "We want jobs, not dole", and threw firecrackers. There were scuffles and some windows were smashed but otherwise there was little trouble.

"Juppe -- we want our pay" shouted protestors from the Vilvoorde site, addressing French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whom workers hope can influence Renault. The French state still holds a 46 percent stake in the car maker.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in Vilvoorde, discussed the Renault closure with Juppe by telephone on Monday, but declined to reveal the outcome.
"C4. Merci Louis," read one placard, referring to the form Belgians must complete to claim unemployment benefit and to Renault boss Louis Schweitzer.
Unions accuse Schweitzer of closing a profitable plant with high labour flexibility and of protecting jobs in France at less profitable and less efficient units.

Belgian authorities joined demonstrators in calling the decision brutal and unacceptable. The federal government and the government of the northern Flanders region said they would sue Renault over the procedure it followed in announcing the closure.
A spokesman for Flemish Economics Minister Eric Van Rompuy said Renault breached Belgian and European Union (EU) rules on informing and consulting staff on strategic decisions.
Under the rules Renault should have told Vilvoorde staff of the planned closure ahead of time and workers should have been asked for advice on the plan.

Dehaene said in a letter to European Commission chairman Jacques Santer that the EU should make such surprise cross-border company closures harder. Renault's decision to shut Vilvoorde had hit Belgium "at a particularly tough time with respect to unemployment", he said.

Dehaene later told a meeting in Brussels on the single currency that "individual countries are powerless in the face of cross-border operations. Only coordinated action on a European level can bring any relief".
In Paris eight unions from Belgium, France and Spain called the one-hour strike and said they also planned to take legal steps to thwart the decision to close Vilvoorde.

"(We call) for a one-hour strike at all Renault sites in Belgium, Spain and France on March 7 during the day of action in the entire Belgian car industry against the Vilvoorde closure," the unions' statement said.
A Renault spokeswoman said Schweitzer had agreed to meet staff this week at the Belgian plant, but the time and place had not been set.

She had no comment on newspaper reports that it was preparing to announce a plan to cut about 3,000 jobs in France this year. But an industry source said somewhat fewer than 3,000 posts would go in 1997.
Renault is closing Vilvoorde in July as part of a reorganisation of production designed to save it 825 million French francs ($140 million) a year.

Belgian workers said the main aim of the protests was to keep the hi-tech plant open. But Luk Siebens, a 30-year-old single parent who had worked at Renault for the last 15 years, said he was resigned to losing his job. "I'm a realist", he told Reuters.

Vilvoorde workers are holding 5,000 finished cars worth three billion Belgian francs ($86 million) hostage. The site contains 10 billion francs of equipment and 2,000 semi-finished cars. It contains the moulds for the Megane Coupe D -- Vilvoorde is the only site where the model is made.
By waging a publicity war against Renault, unions hope to dent its image and thus affect car sales.
On Thursday Schweitzer will attend a works council meeting in Paris to face angry French workers.

Renault has four assembly plants in France, two in Spain, one in Portugal and one in Slovenia. In Paris Renault shares lost 4.7 percent to 140 francs due to profit-taking after having risen 20 percent since last Wednesday. REUTER
